title: The Phone Company That Offered the CIA $1 Million
subtitle: The rejected offer, the private channels, and the papers that made the relationship public.
description:
In 1970, an American company offered the CIA $1 million to keep Salvador Allende out of Chile’s presidency. The offer was rejected. The relationship did not end there.

ITT owned telephone networks, Sheraton hotels, and the company behind Wonder Bread. This documentary follows the former CIA director on its board, campaign funding, economic-pressure proposals, leaked memoranda and Senate questioning—and what became of the investment its executives were trying to protect.

Based on U.S. Senate investigations, declassified government records and official insurance records. The political contacts of 1970 and the military coup of 1973 are distinct events. Dollar figures are nominal U.S. dollars.

Full visual credits, source licenses and modifications: https://github.com/Lucascristao/Plotquake/blob/main/docs/ITT_VISUAL_CREDITS.md

acts.title: The Door Into Washington
acts.subtitle: An offer is refused. Contacts continue.

scenes.caption: 1970 | The offer
scenes.narration: One million dollars. In 1970, International Telephone and Telegraph offered that amount to the CIA to help keep Salvador Allende out of Chile's presidency. The agency rejected the offer. Yet a later Senate investigation found that other ITT money had reached a presidential campaign, with CIA advice on secret channels. A refusal had not ended the relationship. To understand what happened, follow the people who could pick up the phone.

scenes.caption: John McCone | A director on both sides of the connection
scenes.narration: John McCone had run the CIA under Presidents Kennedy and Johnson. By 1970, he sat on ITT's board. When the company wanted to reach American intelligence, it had someone who knew the institution from the director's chair. McCone contacted Richard Helms, the serving intelligence chief. Further contacts brought ITT together with William Broe, the agency's head of Western Hemisphere operations. A concern about a telephone investment could now be discussed with officials whose work included covert political action.

visualPlan.caption: U.S. Senate report · 1973 · McCone and Helms

scenes.caption: July 1970 | Geneen meets Broe
scenes.narration:
In July, before Chileans voted, ITT chairman Harold Geneen met Broe. The company wanted the CIA to channel substantial private business money to Jorge Alessandri, the conservative candidate running against Allende. Broe said no. Agency rules at that stage allowed an operation against Allende's coalition, but not direct support for a particular presidential candidate. That distinction mattered inside the institution. To an executive seeking a practical route for his money, it left another possibility. Broe consulted the CIA station in Santiago, where a funding channel already existed. The station's officers had advised on its security. At a second July meeting, Broe brought Geneen that information.

ITT would have to move its own money. It could receive guidance from people who knew the channels. This account comes from a CIA briefing prepared for congressional testimony in 1972. Even the agency's own explanation acknowledged advice after the refusal. The immediate boundary concerned who would handle the funds. It did not end the company's search for a way to influence the election. Geneen had a business in Chile that he could neither move home nor simply ignore.

acts.title: The Business at Stake
acts.subtitle: A corporate empire confronts an election.

scenes.caption: Chile | A network that could not leave
scenes.narration: The investment was built into the country: cables, exchanges, equipment, and the everyday work of connecting customers. A telephone company cannot respond to a hostile political climate by packing up its network. Its assets remain inside the borders of the government it is negotiating with. That made Chile's election unusually important to ITT. Allende's Popular Unity coalition proposed a socialist transformation, including national control of major industries and services. For the corporation, that could mean losing command of an operating business. For supporters of nationalization, control over essential services was part of what political change was meant to accomplish.

visualPlan.caption: American telephone industry · Bell System, late 1950s
A BUSINESS THAT COULD NOT LEAVE

scenes.caption: Harold Geneen | The reach of the conglomerate
scenes.narration: Geneen was accustomed to enlarging ITT by buying companies. He had taken command in 1959; the corporation's later history credits his era with more than three hundred fifty acquisitions between 1960 and 1977. Sheraton joined ITT in 1968. The wider empire also included Hartford insurance and Continental Baking, associated with Wonder Bread. You could encounter the company in a hotel or a supermarket without thinking about a telephone. Headquarters brought these businesses together through ownership, management, and financial reporting. Chile presented a different kind of problem. Another acquisition could add earnings. It could not settle who should control a network in a country preparing to choose its president.

visualPlan.caption: American telephone industry · Bell System, late 1950s

scenes.caption: An investment and a Cold War election
scenes.narration: Washington saw the election through the Cold War. American officials feared an expansion of Marxist influence in the hemisphere. ITT had property and income at stake. Those interests could bring the same people into the same conversation without making their objectives identical. The United States had its own reasons to oppose Allende. Chilean parties had their own constituencies and rivalries. McCone's access gave Geneen a way into that struggle; it did not give the company authority over everyone involved.

visualPlan.caption: Nixon and Kissinger · 1970 White House photograph
American telephone industry · Bell System, late 1950s

scenes.caption: The Senate's finding | At least $350,000
scenes.narration: At least three hundred fifty thousand dollars from ITT reached Alessandri's campaign, the Senate's 1975 investigation found. The agency had declined to handle the company's money. Its officers had nevertheless advised on secure funding mechanisms, including a channel involving agency assets. ITT could help its preferred candidate without the agency handling the transfer. The agency had refused to take custody of corporate funds. ITT had still found a way to send money to the campaign. Geneen's company had found a route into the election. The result would still depend on Chilean voters.

acts.title: The Weeks Between Votes
acts.subtitle: The popular vote changes the objective.

scenes.caption: September 4, 1970 | The voters decide
scenes.narration:
Allende finished first, with about thirty-six percent of the popular vote. He had won a plurality rather than a majority. Under Chile's constitutional process, Congress would choose between the leading candidates. The custom favored the candidate with the most votes, but the formal decision was still weeks away. For Allende and his supporters, that interval stood between an electoral victory and taking office. For his opponents, it offered a remaining opportunity. ITT had failed to secure the outcome it wanted at the polls. Now its contacts turned toward the next decision.

One proposed maneuver called for Congress to select Alessandri, who would resign and make way for a new election. Outgoing President Eduardo Frei could then run against Allende. There was an immediate difficulty: Alessandri had said before the vote that he would not accept the presidency unless he finished first. A contemporary CIA analysis doubted that the maneuver would work. The route existed on paper, with a central participant publicly committed against it.

visualPlan.caption: Eduardo Frei and his cabinet · circa 1966

scenes.caption: September 1970 | Another million-dollar proposal
scenes.narration: Geneen now offered a million dollars toward a United States government plan to assemble a coalition in Chile's Congress and keep Allende from taking office. McCone carried the proposal to Helms and Henry Kissinger, according to the Senate's 1973 findings. Before the election, the company had sought a way to fund Alessandri's campaign. Now the votes had been cast, and the chairman was offering to support an operation aimed at the remaining congressional decision. He was still seeking Washington's help, with weeks left before Chile's lawmakers chose the president.

scenes.caption: Washington's separate operation
scenes.narration: American officials were already acting on their own. At a September fifteenth White House meeting, Helms recorded ten million dollars available, more if necessary, and a demand for a plan within forty-eight hours. Those notes describe resources made available, not a final spending account. The government pursued a parliamentary route and a separate military route. A CIA message ordered that the military operation be hidden even from the American ambassador and State Department. Officials dealing with the congressional option could therefore be excluded from another operation against the same candidate. ITT was approaching a government pursuing its own secret policies, with resources far beyond the company's proposed contribution.

visualPlan.caption: Nixon and Kissinger · 1970 White House photograph

scenes.caption: A proposal the company would not follow
scenes.narration: The CIA then brought ITT a proposal of its own: help create economic chaos in Chile. Geneen, McCone, and executive Edward Gerrity considered it and rejected it as impractical, the Senate later found. A diplomatic cable from the crisis recorded other suggestions involving credit, orders, and spare parts. Such pressure would reach a country through ordinary business operations. A firm unable to renew a loan might reduce activity. Equipment could become harder to maintain if parts were delayed. These were mechanisms being proposed during the crisis. ITT's leaders declined the agency's plan while continuing to seek a way to stop Allende.

visualPlan.caption: U.S. Senate report · 1973 · proposals and rejection
American telephone industry · Bell System, late 1950s

scenes.caption: The objective fails
scenes.narration: On October twenty-fourth, Chile's Congress confirmed Allende. He was inaugurated on November third. ITT now had to deal with the president its executives had tried to prevent from taking office. McCone's access, the campaign funding, and the proposed million dollars had not stopped him.

scenes.caption: Negotiating the price
scenes.narration: Keeping Allende out had failed. Negotiating over the assets remained possible. The Senate's account describes a striking gap between the sides: ITT sought a valuation of one hundred fifty-three million dollars for its telephone interest; Chile offered twenty-four million. These were positions in a negotiation, not an agreed measure of what the company had lost. The dispute also concerned who would manage the business during a proposed arbitration over its value. That condition mattered because a long negotiation could leave ownership unresolved while someone still had to run the network. Chile intervened in the telephone company's management in 1971. The commercial conflict had become a contest over both the price of an investment and control of the operation while the price was being argued.

visualPlan.caption: American telephone industry · Bell System, late 1950s
U.S. Senate report · 1973 · the telephone investment

scenes.caption: October 1, 1971 | The eighteen-point letter
scenes.narration: On October first, 1971, William Merriam sent an eighteen-point plan to Peter Peterson, a White House economic adviser. Geneen had instructed Merriam to put suggestions in writing after contacts in Washington, the Senate report says. A year earlier, Geneen and his colleagues had rejected the CIA's economic-chaos proposal as impractical. Now the company's own Washington office was proposing American economic pressure on Allende's government. ITT was pursuing negotiations over its Chilean property while seeking leverage through the United States. Peterson later testified that he took no measures to implement the plan.

visualPlan.caption: U.S. Senate report · 1973 · Broe approaches Gerrity

scenes.caption: The possibility of a settlement
scenes.narration: At the same time, company representatives were still discussing a negotiated solution with Chile. The Senate report describes an effort to arrange an international assessment of the telephone company's value. Senior executive Edward Guilfoyle and Chilean official Orlando Letelier were involved in talks. A valuation process offered a way to turn the confrontation into a negotiation over terms. But ITT's internal memoranda contained a history that was about to become public.

scenes.caption: March 1972 | The memoranda become public
scenes.narration:
Jack Anderson began publishing revelations from internal ITT documents in March 1972. The memoranda connected an American corporation to efforts against a Chilean presidential candidate. They also reached the people discussing the company's financial future. ITT executives later told Senate investigators that publication interrupted the international valuation effort and the Guilfoyle-Letelier meeting. The company was seeking an acceptable settlement from a government it had worked to keep out of power. Now records of those efforts were public while its property remained in dispute.

Chile's government translated the memoranda into Spanish and made them available in an inexpensive paperback. Papers written for a small executive circle could be read by the people whose political future had been discussed. Washington officials described the disclosures as a policy setback and a political gain for Allende. A separate memorandum noted the damage to Chile's opposition. The records had traveled from corporate offices into a struggle over public opinion, where Allende could use them to make his case against foreign interference.

scenes.caption: April 18, 1972 | A wider expropriation proposal
scenes.narration: On April eighteenth, Allende announced that he would ask Congress to expropriate all ITT holdings in Chile. The telephone company's management was already under state control from the previous year's intervention. This announcement concerned legislation and a wider range of holdings. The corporation was facing the consequences of public disclosure while the conflict over its property continued.

scenes.caption: 1973 | Who initiated the calls?
scenes.narration: Investigators began putting the documents beside the participants' explanations. Who had initiated the contacts? Broe said ITT's Washington representative, Merriam, had called him. The company's account placed the initiative on the CIA side. Investigators then raised a memorandum recording a call from Broe to another ITT employee. Broe said he did not recall it; if it had happened, he suggested, he might have thought he was speaking to Merriam. Questioning also turned to economic pressure. Broe denied discussing a run on Chilean banks and said he had not developed an action plan with ITT. He nevertheless acknowledged taking the initiative in discussing economic pressure to hasten Chile's deterioration. A State Department memorandum preserves officials' account of this questioning, including the denials and the acknowledgment.

scenes.caption: Church puts the interference in American terms
scenes.narration: Church asked McCone to imagine the situation reversed. Suppose a British oil company helped finance efforts to prevent the candidate with the most votes from becoming president of the United States. How would he view that interference? McCone expressed strong concern. Church's hypothetical brought the issue home to an American audience. The corporate officials had discussed investment, channels, and the limits of agency policy. The senator asked them to consider what their conduct meant for a country's choice of president. A telephone network was property with a negotiable price. The people using it also had a government to choose.

visualPlan.caption: U.S. Senate report · 1973 · corporate conduct and sovereignty

scenes.caption: March 1973 | The insurance claim
scenes.narration: ITT also had a political-risk insurance claim to pursue. The American institution handling it, the Overseas Private Investment Corporation, or OPIC, faced a decision over ninety-two and a half million dollars. In March 1973, a memorandum to Kissinger described management's proposal to refuse the claim. OPIC's managers believed the company's revealed activities had prejudiced their institution's rights under its contract. The same political efforts intended to help protect ITT's property were now being weighed against its request for compensation. Public disclosure had reached beyond reputations and negotiations into the company's attempt to recover money under an American insurance agreement.

visualPlan.caption: American telephone industry · Bell System, late 1950s

scenes.caption: September 11, 1973 | Chile under military rule
scenes.narration: On September eleventh, 1973, the Chilean military overthrew Allende. The presidential palace came under attack. Allende died, and military rule began. Three years had passed since ITT tried to prevent his inauguration. The dictatorship brought torture, disappearances, and other grave violations later examined by international human-rights bodies. Chilean families would live with losses and demands for justice that extended far beyond the financial disputes of foreign companies. The country whose political future had been discussed in corporate memoranda had entered a long period of military rule.

scenes.caption: What the record establishes
scenes.narration: In its 2000 report to Congress, the CIA acknowledged trying to instigate a coup in 1970. For 1973, it described knowledge of military plotting and relationships with some plotters, while saying it had not instigated that coup. That is the agency's later account of its own role. The record examined here establishes ITT's offers, political funding, contacts, and pressure proposals during the earlier struggle. It does not establish that ITT paid for the 1973 takeover. The rejected million-dollar offer cannot be converted into a completed purchase of that later event.

acts.title: The Fate of the Investment
acts.subtitle: The insurance dispute and the surviving company.

scenes.caption: The insurance dispute continues
scenes.narration: ITT continued pursuing compensation for its Chilean investment. The March 1973 memorandum anticipated that the company might challenge a refusal through arbitration. Its financial claim would have a later outcome: OPIC's official ledger records compensation for the ITT case in fiscal 1975. The company had lost control of its operation, and the controversy over its conduct had reached Congress. It still had an insurance claim tied to that property.

visualPlan.caption: FRUS · later editorial note on the insurance settlement
U.S. Senate report · 1973 · the insurance controversy

scenes.caption: 1975 | Cash and guarantees
scenes.narration: Approximately ninety-four-point-one million dollars appears in the official ledger for the ITT case. About thirty-four-point-seven million was cash. Another fifty-nine-point-four million took the form of guarantees, financial commitments rather than immediate cash payments. The record divides the compensation between those two forms. ITT had sought American help before the election, then negotiated over the value and management of its property, then pursued insurance. By 1975, that last route had produced a financial result. The company had lost control of its Chilean operation and obtained compensation after its political efforts became public.

visualPlan.caption: Official OPIC claims ledger · Fiscal 1975 settlement
American telephone industry · Bell System, late 1950s

scenes.caption: A surviving company
scenes.narration: ITT continued operating. The Chile controversy did not bankrupt the conglomerate. Its eventual division into three independent public companies was completed in December 1995, through a separate corporate reorganization. Insurance, manufacturing, and hospitality businesses continued beyond the old umbrella. That later breakup closes the conglomerate's history; it does not explain the secret approaches of 1970 or establish that the Chile scandal caused the separation.

scenes.caption: The line the documents revealed
scenes.narration: The CIA's refusal did not stop ITT from funding a campaign with advice about channels. The company's access did not stop Allende from becoming president. Pressure continued, negotiations faltered, and internal papers gave outsiders a record the participants would have to explain. Those are different outcomes, produced by people whose interests sometimes converged and sometimes collided. The million-dollar offer draws attention because it brings corporate money and intelligence power into a single proposal. The rest of the record shows what that proposal alone cannot: how the relationship worked, what it failed to achieve, and how the effort to defend a business became a public argument over another country's right to choose its government.

sources.note: Primary Senate findings, printed pp.12–14: ITT approaches, rejected million-dollar offer, advice on secure channels and at least $350,000 to the Alessandri campaign. The amount offered is not treated as a payment accepted by CIA. Accessed 2026-10-16.

sources.title: U.S. Senate, The International Telephone and Telegraph Company and Chile, 1970–71, 1973
sources.note: Primary investigation, conclusions printed pp.16–17: substantial July offer rejected; separate September $1 million proposal transmitted by McCone to Kissinger and Helms; economic-chaos proposal considered and rejected; early-1971 corporate pressure. Original government PDF downloaded and the relevant conclusions rasterized directly for the film. No fabricated quotation is used.

sources.title: FRUS E–16, Document 104: CIA memorandum, Background for Chilean Hearings, March 21, 1972
sources.note: Contemporary CIA briefing prepared for congressional testimony. Records July 16/27 Geneen–Broe meetings, refusal to channel corporate funds, advice on secure channels and policy against direct candidate support. This is a defensive agency account, not an independent finding; inconsistent denials elsewhere in it are not repeated as settled history.

sources.title: FRUS E–16, Document 131: memorandum describing CIA discussions with Church's investigators, March 19, 1973
sources.note: Primary State Department memorandum recording CIA officials' account of questioning. Contains disputes about initiative, economic pressure and discrepancies between memoranda and recollections. Reported denials are not converted into proof that alleged events never occurred.

sources.title: ITT, 2011 investor presentation, Heritage of Disciplined Value Creation, slide 19
sources.note: Company-authored SEC-filed primary record: 1920 creation, more than 350 acquisitions in the 1960–1977 Geneen era, subsequent Araskog leadership and 1995 three-way separation. Acquisitions are not described as 350 companies still simultaneously owned. No immediate causal link is drawn between the Chile scandal and the 1995 breakup.

sources.title: ITT Destinations, 1995 distribution prospectus
sources.note: Primary corporate prospectus: Sheraton wholly owned since 1968; over 45 million customers in 60 countries in 1994. Customer stays are presented as the company's reported figure, not unique individuals. Document also provides hospitality portfolio context.

sources.note: Official agency chronology confirms McCone's November 1961–April 1965 tenure and the presidents he served. Career context is not evidence of personal involvement in every later agency operation.

sources.note: Contemporary post-election analysis provides the popular-vote result, parliamentary choice, historical precedent and Alessandri-resignation/Frei-election scenario. Allende's share is rounded to about 36 percent; he did not win a majority.

sources.note: Primary interagency assessment calls the Anderson–ITT documents a policy setback and political gain for Allende. Its strategic assessment is attributed to American officials, not made into a quantified estimate of electoral impact.

sources.note: Official documentary-edition chronology cites primary archives for Anderson disclosures beginning March 21, 1972 and the Senate inquiry. Its compressed April 18 expropriation wording is clarified by the contemporary S23 memorandum, used for the expropriation chronology.

sources.note: Primary corporate report confirms December 19, 1995 distribution to shareholders of ITT Destinations and ITT Hartford, and continued ITT Industries operations. The corporation's separation is not described as a court-ordered breakup or a bankruptcy.

sources.note: Official edition transcribes primary handwritten notes recording $10 million available, more if necessary, and 48 hours for a plan. Available resources are not represented as money actually spent or as ITT's money. No verbatim quotation is used.

sources.note: Contemporary memorandum records a proposed rejection of ITT's $92.5 million claim on contractual grounds. The official edition's later editorial note records 1975 compensation; the separate DFC ledger S25 supplies the cash and guarantee amounts. No conclusion about liability for Chile's 1973 coup is inferred.
